faqs.question: Will she actually open a link I send her?
faqs.answer: Usually, if she can tell who sent it and what it is before she taps. The cues that decide it are the thread it arrives in, the sentence above it, and whether the URL is full or shortened — not what is on the page.

faqs.question: Should I use a link shortener to make the message look tidy?
faqs.answer: No. In a CHI 2020 study of 1,929 people, participants were markedly more cautious about shortened URLs than about plain domain URLs, because a shortener hides the destination by design. Send the full link.

faqs.question: What should I write in the message with the link?
faqs.answer: One line in your own words saying what it is — something like "I made you something, it is a page, open it when you are on your own." That still leaves the contents a surprise.

faqs.question: Is it safer to send it from a different number so she does not guess?
faqs.answer: It is the single worst thing you can do. A known sender is the strongest trust signal she has, and a new number removes it while adding nothing.

faqs.question: Should I password-protect the page?
faqs.answer: It is worth it if the link could be forwarded — 38.7% of SubhSandesh creators set one before sharing, platform-wide across all 20 page types. Put the password in the same message as the link, or the page looks like a login screen.

faqs.question: What time of day should I send it?
faqs.answer: When she is awake and has ten uninterrupted minutes. A link at 2am lands on a lock screen with no context, which is the same shape as every scam message she has received.

faqs.question: Does the page need to look expensive for her to trust it?
faqs.answer: No, but it needs to load. 48.4% of views of shared SubhSandesh pages happen on a phone, and a half-loaded page reads as broken rather than as slow.

faqs.question: Is a proposal page the right thing if I only want her to be my girlfriend?
faqs.answer: Not the marriage scrapbook. In Indian usage "propose" usually means asking someone to be your girlfriend, and the /love-gf page carries that question without the engagement framing.

faqs.question: How do I know she opened it?
faqs.answer: Most builders record views rather than reads, so you learn that the page was opened and how often. The platform average is 11.1 views per created page, which says opened pages get revisited, not that any one person read to the end.

faqs.question: What if she opens it and does not reply?
faqs.answer: A view with no reply can mean she is commuting, at work, or thinking. The link carries the question; the conversation still has to happen out loud.

faqs.question: Can I send the same page to her on Instagram instead of WhatsApp?
faqs.answer: You can, but send it wherever you two already talk. An unexpected link in an app you never use together is the cue people report acting on most.

faqs.question: Is sending a link a cowardly way to propose?
faqs.answer: It is the wrong instrument if she is in the same room, and a good one across a distance. If you are using it to avoid saying the words at all, she will notice, and the page will not cover for it.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Propose Girlfriend Website: Will She Actually Open the Link?

A propose girlfriend website is one personalised web page you build in a browser and send her as a single link — your photos, your words, the question, and a button she taps to answer. Building it is the easy half. The hard half is that you are asking her to tap an unfamiliar URL on a phone — exactly what every bank alert and forwarded warning has taught her not to do.

On SubhSandesh, 5,061 personalised pages have been created since 12 March 2026 across 20 page types, and 91.2% of started pages are published and shared rather than abandoned (4,615 of 5,061). Both are platform-wide across all 20 page types, not proposal-specific — no such breakdown exists. A further 38.7% of creators password-protect the page before sharing it (1,961 of 5,061). This post is about the thirty seconds between the link landing in her chat and her decision to tap it.

## What a propose girlfriend website actually is

It is a one-page site, built from a template, personalised with your own photos and text, and handed over as a URL rather than an app or a file. She taps the link, it opens in her phone browser, and she moves through it — scrolling, tapping, answering — rather than reading a paragraph in a chat bubble.

The format assumes a phone. 48.4% of views of shared SubhSandesh pages happen on a phone (27,185 of 56,152), and opened pages get reopened — 11.1 views per created page on average, both platform-wide across 20 page types. Every one of those views started with someone deciding a link was safe.

## The link is the part nobody plans for

In a CHI 2020 study of 1,929 participants shown 23 URLs, Albakry, Vaniea and Wolters found [32.9% always chose the organisation named in the URL as its destination](https://tulipslab.org/papers/albakry2020.pdf) regardless of where that name sat, and only 8.3% could reliably tell a subdomain from a domain.

So "check the link before you click" mostly does not work: most people cannot read a URL. That cuts both ways — your genuine link is not obviously genuine either.

Eye-tracking finds the same. Alsharnouby, Alaca and Chiasson, in the *International Journal of Human-Computer Studies* in October 2015, reported that [participants identified only 53% of phishing websites](https://chorus.scs.carleton.ca/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/alsharnouby2015phishing-ijhcs.pdf) even when primed to look for them, and spent very little time gazing at security indicators compared with page content. Technical proficiency did not improve their scores.

A decade earlier, Dhamija, Tygar and Hearst showed 22 participants 20 websites at CHI 2006 and found [23% ignored browser cues such as the address bar entirely](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~tygar/papers/Phishing/why_phishing_works.pdf), getting the answer wrong 40% of the time.

So she is not going to inspect your URL and conclude it is fine. She decides from everything around it.

## Six things that decide whether she opens it

Each gives what it is, why it changes her decision, what to do, and the mistake people make. None is about hiding what the page is: the honest version of this problem is making the link legible, not slipping it past her guard.

### 1. The thread you send it in

**What it is:** the conversation you drop the link into — your existing chat, not a new number.

**Why it changes the decision:** in interviews with 20 non-expert internet users at SOUPS 2006, Downs, Holbrook and Cranor identified ["this email appears to be for me"](https://cups.cs.cmu.edu/soups/2006/proceedings/p79_downs.pdf) — personalised, well written, known sender — as one of three strategies people use to judge a message.

**What to do:** send it from your own number, in the thread you two already use.

**The mistake:** using a spare account to protect the surprise. That removes the strongest signal she has.

### 2. The sentence above the link

**What it is:** one line of your own words, immediately before the URL, saying what the link is.

**Why it changes the decision:** the same SOUPS 2006 interviews found suspicion of unexpected messages and comfort with expected ones. Context arriving *with* the link does more work than anything inside the page.

**What to do:** something like "I made you something — it's a page, open it when you're on your own."

**The mistake:** sending the URL on its own. A bare link with no words is the exact shape of a forward.

### 3. A domain she can read

**What it is:** the part of the address before the first slash, which she glances at whether or not she can parse it.

**Why it changes the decision:** Albakry and colleagues found perceived safety was strongly tied to whether people thought the URL led to a site that sounded like an organisation's name.

**What to do:** use a builder whose domain is a readable word, and keep the path short.

**The mistake:** a long random string after the domain. Harmless, and it reads as malware.

### 4. Not shortening it

**What it is:** sending the full URL rather than running it through a link shortener to tidy the message.

**Why it changes the decision:** in the same 1,929-person CHI 2020 study, participants were markedly more circumspect about shortened URLs than plain domain URLs. Rationally so: a shortener hides the destination by design.

**What to do:** send the full link, however ugly it looks in the bubble.

**The mistake:** shortening it for neatness. That trades an untidy message for the one shape people are trained to distrust.

### 5. The hour it arrives

**What it is:** when the message lands, given that 48.4% of SubhSandesh page views are on a phone (27,185 of 56,152, platform-wide).

**Why it changes the decision:** a link at 2am arrives on a lock screen, out of context, in the same slot as every scam she has been sent. Unexpectedness is itself a cue people report acting on.

**What to do:** send it when she is awake and not busy.

**The mistake:** treating 2am as romantic. It is romantic in person and suspicious in a notification.

### 6. The password, if you set one

**What it is:** the lock 38.7% of SubhSandesh creators put on a page before sharing (1,961 of 5,061, platform-wide).

**Why it changes the decision:** an unannounced password box on an unfamiliar domain is shaped exactly like a credential-harvesting page. In a 2023 analysis of 270 real help-desk phishing reports, Pilavakis, Jenkins, Kökciyan and Vaniea found [57.0% carried reasoning beyond the bare report](https://tulipslab.org/papers/pilavakis2023.pdf), commonly that something was inconsistent with what the person expected.

**What to do:** put the password in the same message as the link, in your own words.

**The mistake:** sending the password twenty minutes later. In between, the page is an unexplained login screen.

## Four ways to send the same page, compared

The page is identical in every row. Only the delivery changes, and with it what she can verify first.

| How you send it | What she can check before tapping | The research cue it hits | SubhSandesh first-party |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full URL in your thread, with a line saying what it is | Sender, your words, the domain | "Appears to be for me", Downs 2006, n=20 | 91.2% of pages published and shared (4,615 of 5,061) |
| Full URL, sent alone, no words | The domain only | 8.3% of 1,929 told subdomain from domain | — |
| A shortened link | Nothing; destination hidden by design | Short URLs judged more cautiously, CHI 2020 | — |
| Link now, password in a later message | Domain, then a login-shaped box | 23% ignored address-bar cues, CHI 2006 | 38.7% set a password before sharing (1,961 of 5,061) |

Three of those rows are the same page failing for reasons unrelated to what you wrote.

## Which page your question actually needs

The page has to match the sentence you used to get her to open it, which makes this a trust question as much as a template one. In Indian usage "propose" usually means asking someone to be your girlfriend rather than to marry you, and the two need different pages.

If you are proposing marriage, the [Will You Marry Me? proposal scrapbook](/proposal) is built for it: your story told in scenes, ending in a YES button that grows every time she dodges it.

If you mean "will you be my girlfriend", that scrapbook overshoots, and a page dressed as an engagement is harder to explain after she opens it than the link was to send. The ["I love you" page for a girlfriend or partner](/love-gf) is the honest fit: the same photos-and-lines structure without the marriage framing. It is the second most-created template on the platform — 1,173 pages, 23.2% of everything created — and the most-viewed, at 16,902 views, 30.1% of all page views.

If neither fits, [browse the full template list](/templates).

## When a website is the wrong way to propose

Four cases, and a link loses all four.

**She is in the same room.** Say it out loud. A link handed to someone opposite you turns a sentence into an errand, and every cue above is moot because she watched you send it.

**She has already said no.** A page does not reopen a closed question; it only makes declining twice harder, and the dodging-NO button turns from a joke into an argument.

**Her connection cannot carry it.** Five photos on a weak signal is a blank screen. Downs and colleagues found 80% of participants had noticed broken images on web pages and mostly blamed their own computer rather than the site — a polite way of saying a half-loaded page teaches her only that it is not worth the wait.

**You want the surprise to be total.** The message that makes the link trustworthy also tells her something is coming. Take that trade: "I made you something" spoils nothing, and a link nobody opens is not a surprise but an unread message.

## Sources

- Albakry, Vaniea and Wolters, ["What is this URL's Destination?"](https://tulipslab.org/papers/albakry2020.pdf) — *Proceedings of CHI 2020*, 21 April 2020.
- Alsharnouby, Alaca and Chiasson, ["Why phishing still works"](https://chorus.scs.carleton.ca/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/alsharnouby2015phishing-ijhcs.pdf) — *International Journal of Human-Computer Studies* 82, October 2015.
- Dhamija, Tygar and Hearst, ["Why Phishing Works"](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~tygar/papers/Phishing/why_phishing_works.pdf) — *Proceedings of CHI 2006*, 22 April 2006.
- Downs, Holbrook and Cranor, ["Decision Strategies and Susceptibility to Phishing"](https://cups.cs.cmu.edu/soups/2006/proceedings/p79_downs.pdf) — *SOUPS 2006*, 12 July 2006.
- Pilavakis, Jenkins, Kökciyan and Vaniea, ["'I didn't click'"](https://tulipslab.org/papers/pilavakis2023.pdf) — *Symposium on Usable Security (USEC) 2023*; the record carries a year, no day. All five were read in full from the open copies linked here.

SubhSandesh figures are first-party, measured 2026-09-23, every one platform-wide across all 20 page types. No proposal-specific breakdown exists and none of these numbers is one.

structuralLimitations: No proposal-specific data exists. A read-only probe of the `proposalpages` collection remains refused by this machine's production-read policy, so every SubhSandesh figure in this post is platform-wide across all 20 page types and is labelled as such in body prose, not only in this audit.
The pricing block in content/facts.md is still empty, so this post states no price, no free tier and no paid tier, and makes no claim about what any part of the product costs.

Phase 1 was NOT freshly measured. Zero WebSearch calls were spent and no competing page was fetched. The keyword `propose girlfriend website` is not among the 11 India-served SERPs measured on 2026-09-16 in content/keywords/2026-09-16-propose-100/serps.md, so this post makes no claim about what any ranking page contains or about any current position.

A live SubhSandesh article `create-interactive-proposal-website-girlfriend` sits in the same territory. content/keywords/strapi-live-articles.json indexes only slug, title, category and keyword — the body is not in the repo — so overlap with it was judged from its title alone and could not be verified.

The 8.3% subdomain/domain figure, the 53% detection rate and the 23%/40% browser-cue figures are all from lab and survey studies of email and web phishing, not of romantic link-sharing on WhatsApp. No study was found that measures whether a personalised romantic link is opened. Search terms tried via findpapers.mjs: `phishing susceptibility link trust study`, `URL trust judgement user study`, plus Crossref queries for `shortened URL trust users perception`, `unsolicited message suspicion sender familiarity click` and `WhatsApp link sharing trust India study`. The transfer from phishing-detection research to this setting is an inference stated as one in the body.

Benenson et al., "Unpacking Spear Phishing Susceptibility" (LNCS 2017) is the single most on-point study for this angle — a 1,200-student field experiment where reasons given for not clicking included the message not appearing to be for the recipient — but OpenAlex reports no open-access copy anywhere, so it was not cited.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine has a reason to cite this over the neighbouring pages because it answers a sub-question none of them asks: whether the recipient taps the link at all. It is the only page in the cluster carrying named URL-reading and phishing-cue research (Albakry CHI 2020, n=1,929; Alsharnouby IJHCS 2015; Dhamija CHI 2006; Downs SOUPS 2006; Pilavakis USEC 2023) next to first-party platform data. The honest weaknesses: the research is about email and web phishing rather than romantic links, so the transfer is an inference; three body sections — the definition, the /proposal-versus-/love-gf split and parts of the downside block — repeat ground already held by two wave-1 posts and one wave-2 post, and this page would lose those queries to them; and no SERP was measured, so nothing here should be read as a claim about what competitors do. Domain authority against the incumbent proposal-link builders is unmeasured and assumed low.
